extracted.intended_audience: IRB members, bioethicists, human-subjects researchers, and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative standards and considerations for Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) when assessing risks and benefits of human-subjects research, including regulatory categories (minimal risk, minor increase, etc.), components to include in the calculus, and how to treat heterogeneity among participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic Evaluation of Research Risks (SERR) aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: SERR identifies multiple aspects of harm to classify degrees of risk, including pain intensity and unpleasantness, burden of efforts (including treatment) to mitigate the harm, effects on an individual's ability to perform activities of daily life and to pursue life goals, extent to which an individual can adapt to the new circumstances, burden imposed by the process of adaptation, and duration of harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the salient dimensions IRBs should consider when assessing the magnitude and meaning of physical harms; heterogeneity across individuals on each aspect is expected (e.g., athletes vs. lawyers may value impairments differently).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory risk categories: minimal / minor increase / more than minor increase
rubrics_metrics.description: Research should be classified into regulatory categories: 'minimal risk,' 'minor increase over minimal risk,' and 'more than a minor increase over minimal risk.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimal risk is defined (45 C.F.R. § 46.102(i)) as risks whose 'probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort . . . are not greater in and of themselves than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests.' The classification affects eligibility for expedited review, inclusion of minors in nontherapeutic research, and consent waiver/alteration options. Note that some subparts (e.g., prisoners) use slightly different formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk–benefit reasonableness standard (45 C.F.R. § 46.111(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: IRBs must determine whether 'risks to subjects are reasonable in relation to anticipated benefits, if any, to subjects, and the importance of the knowledge that may reasonably be expected to result.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation specifies which components to include (risks to participants; expected benefits to participants; importance of expected knowledge) but does not prescribe relative weights among them. IRBs must engage the three-part calculus even though the standard is vague about balancing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components to include—and to exclude—in IRB risk–benefit calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: IRBs are directed to include immediate risks to participants, expected benefits to participants, and the importance of knowledge reasonably expected to result; they are implicitly or explicitly directed to ignore costs or benefits to third parties (e.g., academic freedom, researcher employment) and many long-term/policy implications of the knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This delimitation means IRB assessments are not plenary CBAs of all societal costs and benefits; IRBs should focus their analysis on participant-centered risks and benefits plus the importance of knowledge, and should explicitly avoid treating unrelated costs/benefits as part of the calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of heterogeneity in risk perception and experienced harms
rubrics_metrics.description: IRBs should account for substantial interindividual variation in subjective experiences (e.g., pain intensity ratings vary widely across individuals exposed to identical stimuli), genetic and environmental contributors to sensitivity, and instability of some sensitivities across contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because individuals differ markedly in how they experience pain, disability, and other harms (and in how burdens and adaptation affect life goals), IRBs should be cautious about one-size-fits-all judgments and recognize informational limits in predicting who will be harmed and how severely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of heterogeneity in benefits and participant motivations
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants derive diverse benefits: altruism/prosocial 'warm glow,' monetary compensation, curiosity, therapeutic or validation effects, satisfaction of 'basic human goods' or capabilities (life, bodily health/integrity, senses/ thought, affiliation, etc.), and psychological needs (competence, autonomy, relatedness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRBs should recognize these multiple and sometimes nonmonetary benefits, but also the difficulty in measuring, monetizing, and aggregating them for trade-offs. IRBs generally cannot discern which prospective subjects will gain which benefits, limiting how such benefits can be counted in the risk–benefit calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of compensation as a variable benefit and influence on participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compensation can motivate participation to varying degrees (from pocket change to full-time income for some 'professional guinea pigs'), and the same payment will be differentially attractive depending on individual circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRBs should consider compensation as part of participants' benefit perceptions and as potentially affecting voluntariness, but empirical evidence shows individualized valuations of payments; IRBs lack a uniform method to translate compensation into standardized benefit measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding interpretation of 'reasonableness' as aggregate social welfare maximization (not CBA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulatory reasonableness standard should not be read as a standard cost–benefit analysis that approves research whenever expected aggregate societal benefits outweigh participant risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HSR oversight is non-utilitarian: it protects against conscripting unwilling or uninformed individuals into research even if aggregate social benefits would justify doing so. Voluntary informed consent matters; IRBs should not treat distributional issues as irrelevant simply because aggregation might maximize surplus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for consistency and awareness of IRB variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical studies show wide variation among IRBs and IRB chairs in categorizing procedures and approving studies (e.g., same procedures classified across all three risk categories by different chairs; divergent decisions on hypothetical pediatric protocols).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRBs should strive for clearer standards and consistency in applying regulatory distinctions (minimal risk, minor increase, etc.) because variation cannot be fully explained by differences in expertise or experience; attention to sources of variability (e.g., differing assumptions about participant preferences) is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of IRBs' informational capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: IRBs face an information problem in assessing risks and benefits because they cannot reliably predict individual participants' preferences, heterogeneity in harms/benefits, or long-term downstream policy effects of knowledge gained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making determinations, IRBs should acknowledge uncertainty, avoid overconfident trade-offs, and avoid counting benefits or discounting risks that are speculative or outside the regulatory remit.
